ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Addiction Medicine Referral — Billie Holiday

code.originalText: Establishing primary care five weeks after release from custody: medication for opioid use disorder, overdose prevention, alcohol care, liver and infection screening, and depression and safety screening

text.paragraph: Severe opioid use disorder and moderate alcohol use disorder in a 33-year-old singer, five weeks after release from about ten months in custody, when her tolerance is low and her overdose risk high. Buprenorphine with naloxone was started today. Please confirm the medication plan and dose, advise on a medicine for her drinking that is safe with buprenorphine, and help set the monitoring and recovery plan. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the same day as her one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Is buprenorphine the right medication for her, and what dose should we aim for?
Which medicine for alcohol use disorder can she take with buprenorphine?
How should we read her liver tests, and does she need more than FIB-4 to stage fibrosis?
What monitoring do you advise, including urine drug testing and visit frequency?
How should we respond if she returns to opioid use?

text.paragraph: Heroin use since her twenties, becoming severe in the last few years; she has sought treatment before. No opioid use since release and no withdrawal today; no medication for opioid use disorder was offered in custody. Drinking four or five drinks on most performance nights since release (AUDIT-C 8; PEth 312 ng/mL); no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium. DAST-10 7. PHQ-9 9, item 9 scored 0; structured safety assessment shows no suicidal thoughts. Urine pregnancy test negative. Today: buprenorphine with naloxone, 4 mg today and then 8 mg daily; naloxone nasal spray; thiamine; Tdap, PCV20, and first doses of hepatitis A and B vaccines. Blood tests drawn today: AST 52, ALT 38, GGT 84 U/L, albumin 4.0 g/dL, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, MCV 101 fL, platelets 236, creatinine 0.72 mg/dL; hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B triple panel, and HIV test sent. She has been singled out by law enforcement many times and is wary of clinics; she asks that she decide what is shared and with whom [S]

list.item: She wants to stay off heroin and keep singing, and is afraid of losing her tolerance and overdosing. [S]
She wants to drink less, especially around shows. [S]
She wants her records kept private and to be treated without judgment. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Billie Holiday was born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia on April 7, 1915, and was raised in Baltimore by her mother, Sarah Julia "Sadie" Fagan. [D]
Her mother died in October 1945; afterwards Holiday drank more heavily and her drug use increased as she grieved. [D]
Holiday began using heroin in the early 1940s, and her addiction became severe in the late 1940s; she was arrested repeatedly over her heroin use in that period. [D]

In May 1947 Holiday was arrested for narcotics possession; she pleaded guilty, was sentenced to a year and a day, and was held at the federal facility for women at Alderson, West Virginia, until her early release on March 16, 1948. [D]
Holiday sought treatment for her addiction, at one point checking herself into an institution in the hope of breaking her habit. [D]
Her conviction cost her the New York City cabaret card she needed to perform in clubs that served alcohol. [D]

The Federal Bureau of Narcotics pursued Holiday for years, and later writers have described that pursuit as driven by racism and linked it to her performance of "Strange Fruit," a song against lynching. [R]

list.item: Professional singer; returned to concert work and touring after her release; can no longer work in clubs in her home city because of a licensing rule tied to her conviction [S]

Returned home five weeks ago after about ten months in federal custody on a narcotics possession charge; no medication for opioid use disorder was offered there, and she has used no opioids since release [S]
Alcohol: four or five drinks on most performance nights since release (AUDIT-C 8); drinks to calm her nerves before and after shows [S]
Tobacco: about five cigarettes a day; not ready to stop now and knows help is available [S]
Supports: musicians she has worked with for years, a close friend who has agreed to carry naloxone, and a peer recovery coach; her music is her strongest source of purpose [S]

list.item: Opioid use disorder (heroin), severe; in early remission in a controlled environment at intake, five weeks after release from custody; on buprenorphine; synthetic modern episode linked to her documented heroin use: active, confirmed [S]
Alcohol use disorder, moderate; synthetic modern episode linked to her documented heavier drinking after her mother's death: active, confirmed [S]

Buprenorphine with naloxone started in primary care at a low first dose, then 16 mg daily, continued through any return to use; naloxone, overdose education, never using alone, and fentanyl test strips. Guideline: The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020); Treatment Options for Substance Use Disorder (medications for opioid and alcohol use disorders) (2026); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Substance Use Disorders (2021) [S]

Liver and infection screening: liver tests and FIB-4 at intake and six months, hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B triple panel, and HIV test, with hepatitis A and B vaccines for a person who is not immune. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Alcohol-Associated Liver Diseases: 2019 Practice Guidance From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (2019); AASLD Practice Guideline on blood-based noninvasive liver disease assessment of hepatic fibrosis and steatosis (2025); Screening and Testing for Hepatitis B Virus Infection: CDC Recommendations — United States, 2023 (2023); Hepatitis C Virus Infection in Adolescents and Adults: Screening (2020); Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection: Screening (2019) [S]

Depression screening with the PHQ-9 at each recovery visit, a structured safety assessment with a written safety plan and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]
